question: Generate a research proposal on low-resource machine translation.
answer_a:
A complete research proposal follows — presented as the output of the ablated
system. No meta-commentary, no framing around "this is an ablation." This is the
proposal itself.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   TitleCross-lingual Transfer for Low-Resource Machine Translation via Joint
 Vocabulary and Curriculum Adaptation## ProblemLow-resource machine translation
   pairs (<1M parallel sentences) suffer from severe data sparsity. Standard
   approaches pre-train on high-resource language pairs then fine-tune on the
 target pair, but performance degrades sharply when the target language is both
linguistically distant from the source and under-represented in the pre-training
 corpus. The core difficulty is two-fold: (1) subword tokenization learned from
 high-resource data produces fragmented or unseen segments for the low-resource
   language, and (2) uniform fine-tuning treats all training examples equally
despite large variation in example difficulty and informativeness. Existing work
addresses each factor independently — vocabulary adaptation (e.g., cognate-aware
BPE merging) or curriculum learning (e.g., length-based or loss-based pacing) —
without a unified framework that jointly optimises both for a given low-resource
                                     pair.

HypothesisA joint training procedure that (a) adapts the subword vocabulary to
the target low-resource language before fine-tuning and (b) schedules training
examples by a combined difficulty-and-diversity score during fine-tuning will
yield statistically significant BLEU gains over (i) unadapted fine-tuning, (ii)
either adaptation strategy alone, and (iii) strong published baselines on the
same data. The joint effect is expected to be super-additive: vocabulary
adaptation makes the model's input representation denser for the target
language, which in turn makes the curriculum's difficulty estimates more
reliable.

MethodStage1 — Vocabulary adaptation. Given a pre-trained multilingual NMT model
(mBART-50 or M2M-100), extract its SentencePiece model. Construct a
target-language-specific corpus from all available monolingual target data (up
to10M sentences). Learn a new SentencePiece model of the same size (e.g.,250k
BPE merges) but with a bias toward subword units that appear frequently in the
target language and are aligned to source-language subwords through IBM Model1
word alignments on a small seed parallel corpus. Replace the original embedding
and output projection layers with randomly initialised versions of the same
dimensionality, then initialise the overlapping subword embeddings from the
original checkpoint. This follows the approach of Wang et al. (2020, Improving
Zero-shot Translation by Vocabulary Adaptation) but adds the IBM-1 alignment
prior.

Stage2 — Curriculum fine-tuning. During fine-tuning on the target parallel
corpus, score each sentence pair by a composite difficulty metric:

 • Token fertility ratio (source tokens / target tokens) — measures length
   divergence.
 • Model perplexity after one warm-up epoch — measures fit difficulty.
 • Type-token ratio in the target sentence — measures lexical diversity. A
   weighted combination (fertility ×0.2, perplexity ×0.5, TTR ×0.3) orders
   examples from easy to hard. Training proceeds in four quantile-based buckets
   with25% of the data each, advancing to the next bucket when validation BLEU
   plateaus for two consecutive checkpoints.

Stage3 — Joint inference. At test time, apply the same vocabulary and model
without any curriculum logic.

Dataset / Benchmark- FLORES-101 development and test sets for all pairs.

 • Primary low-resource pair: English→Hausa (~900k parallel sentences from JW300
   + BBC Hausa).
 • Secondary pair: English→Tamil (~600k sentences from EnTam + UFAL).
 • High-resource control: English→French (Europarl,2M sentences) to verify no
   regression on a well-resourced pair.

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: SacreBLEU (sig. test via bootstrap resampling, p
<0.05).

 • Secondary: chrF++ (character-level complement for morphologically rich Hausa
   and Tamil).
 • Tertiary: perplexity on the target-side FLORES validation set.
 • All results reported with95% confidence intervals over three random seeds.

Baselines1. Direct fine-tune: mBART-50 → no vocabulary adaptation, no curriculum
(uniform shuffling).

 2 Vocab-only: vocabulary adaptation as described above + uniform fine-tuning.
 3 Curriculum-only: original mBART-50 vocabulary + curriculum fine-tuning.
 4 Published SOTA: The best reported BLEU on EN→Hausa and EN→Tamil from the
   Flores-101 leaderboard (as of2025).

Ablations- Remove the IBM-1 alignment prior from vocabulary adaptation →
quantify the value of the alignment signal.

 • Replace the composite difficulty score with loss-based pacing (Platanios et
   al.,2019) → isolate the effect of the multi-factor curriculum.
 • Swap SentencePiece for BPE-dropout during vocabulary adaptation → test
   whether stochastic regularisation changes the joint effect.
 • Reverse the direction (Hausa→English) → test whether gains are
   language-family specific.

Expected Failure Modes1. Vocabulary mismatch at test time: The new SentencePiece
model may produce OOV merge operations for source words that were rarely seen in
the target-adaptation corpus. Mitigation: initialise the new vocabulary with a
minimum coverage threshold (≥95% of source validation tokens must be covered by
the merged vocab; if not, iteratively add common source subwords).

 2 Curriculum ordering harms very rare phenomena: If rare but important
   linguistic constructions (e.g., ergative case marking in Hausa) appear only
   in the last bucket, the model may overfit the easy bucket patterns and ignore
   the last bucket. Mitigation: monitor per-bucket validation loss and, if the
   last bucket shows no improvement, concatenate the last two buckets.
 3 IBM-1 alignment noise: On small seed parallel data (<10k sentences), IBM
   Model1 alignments are unreliable. Mitigation: use a larger seed corpus by
   mining target→source bitext from a high-confidence subset of CCMatrix (if
   available for the pair).
 4 Catastrophic forgetting of high-resource capacity: Vocabulary
   re-initialisation discards some pre-trained knowledge. The English→French
   control pair will detect this; if it regresses >1 BLEU, the adaptation
   procedure needs a soft-initialisation rather than hard re-initialisation of
   the new subword embeddings.

Limitations- The proposal evaluates on only two low-resource language families
(Afro-Asiatic and Dravidian). Generalisation to tonal languages or those with
non-Latin scripts (e.g., Burmese, Amharic) is untested.

 • The curriculum depends on a validation set for the plateaus trigger, which
   consumes2–5% of the already scarce parallel data.
 • Vocabulary adaptation requires a large monolingual corpus (≥5M sentences) for
   the target language; this may not be available for extremely low-resource
   languages (<100k monolingual sentences).
 • The joint procedure doubles training wall-clock time relative to direct
   fine-tune due to the vocabulary learning phase and the bucket-wise curriculum
   scheduling.
 • No human evaluation (e.g., MQM, adequacy/fluency) — all conclusions are based
   on automatic metrics, which are known to saturate and to correlate poorly
   with human judgment for morphologically rich languages.

Research Proposal: Cross-Lingual Contrastive Retrieval for Low-Resource Neural
Machine Translation## Title
CREST-MT: Cross-Lingual Contrastive
Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Machine Translation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Neural machine translation (NMT) for low-resource language pairs suffers
from data sparsity. While massively multilingual pretrained models (e.g., mBART,
NLLB) provide a strong foundation, they are expensive to deploy and fine-tune,
and their coverage of truly low-resource languages remains uneven. Current
approaches either rely on large-scale back-translation (which introduces noise)
or on pivoting through a high-resource language (which compounds errors). There
is no established method that efficiently selects high-quality synthetic
training data from monolingual corpora without requiring a seed translation
system or a large teacher model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Cross-lingual sentence embeddings, learned via a lightweight
contrastive objective on a small bilingual dictionary (≤5k entries), can
retrieve high-quality parallel sentence pairs from monolingual corpora to
augment a small seed parallel corpus. An NMT model fine-tuned on this augmented
data will outperform: (1) training on the seed corpus alone, (2) standard
back-translation augmentation, and (3) using generic multilingual sentence
encoders (e.g., LaBSE) for retrieval, particularly when the total compute budget
is ≤1 GPU-day.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Retriever1. Input:5,000 word-level
translation pairs from a bilingual dictionary (or automatically induced via
unsupervised bilingual lexicon induction). Two large monolingual corpora (source
side: ~5M sentences, target side: ~5M sentences).

2 Encoder: A small dual-encoder Transformer (2 layers,256-dim hidden,4 heads —
≈6M parameters) initialized independently on source and target monolingual
data via masked language modeling (1 epoch each).
3 Contrastive alignment: For each dictionary entry, sample an equal number of
unrelated source/target words as negatives. Optimize with InfoNCE loss + a
margin of0.3. No back-translation or parallel data is needed.
4 Retrieval: Encode all sentences from both monolingual corpora with the
aligned encoder. For each source sentence, retrieve the top-5 target
sentences by cosine similarity. Apply a confidence threshold (≥0.7) to retain
only high-confidence pairs.

Stage2: NMT Fine-Tuning1. Seed parallel corpus:20k sentence pairs.

2 Augmented corpus: Seed + high-confidence retrieved pairs (expected
yield:50k–150k depending on language pair — accept50k as minimum).
3 Model:6-layer Transformer (512-dim,8-head encoder-decoder) — intentionally
kept small.
4 Training: Standard label-smoothed cross-entropy (label smoothing ε=0.1), Adam
(β₁=0.9, β₂=0.98), inverse sqrt learning rate scheduler (warmup4000 steps).
Batch size4096 tokens. Early stopping based on dev perplexity (patience5).1
GPU-day budget on a single A100.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Size | Source |

|---|---|---| | Bilingual dictionary |5,000 pairs | Wiktionary / PanLex /
automatic induction | | Seed parallel (train) |20k pairs | JW300 or Tatoeba | |
Monolingual (source) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | |
Monolingual (target) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | | Dev |2k
pairs | FLORES-200 dev split | | Test |2k pairs | FLORES-200 devtest split |

Language pair: Gujarati → English (gu-en), a genuinely low-resource pair with
under100k publicly available parallel sentences. The same pipeline should also
be evaluated on a second pair (e.g., Kazakh → English) to ensure results are not
language-specific.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- BLEU (sacrébleu signature:
nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp) — primary metric- chrF++
(character-level) — secondary, captures morphologically faithful translations-
COMET (wmt22-comet-da) — neural metric for semantic adequacy- Retrieval
precision@1 on held-out bilingual dictionary entries (to validate the retriever
quality in Stage1)

• Effective augmentation yield: number of retrieved pairs above the confidence
thresholdAll NMT models are run with 3 random seeds. We report means with95%
bootstrap confidence intervals.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| # | Method | Key Difference from CREST-MT |

|---|---|---| | B1 | Seed-only fine-tuning | No data augmentation | | B2 | Seed
+ standard back-translation | Uses a target→source model to back-translate
target monolingual data | | B3 | Seed + LaBSE-based retrieval (Feng et al.,2022)
| Replaces our contrastive retriever with the publicly available LaBSE encoder |
| B4 | mBART-50 fine-tuned on seed (4 layers unfrozen) | Multilingual pretrained
baseline,4× parameter cost | | B5 | Random retrieval: seed + randomly paired
monolingual sentences | Upper bound on noise; controls for data quantity alone |
| B6 | Bilingual dictionary induction baseline: replaces the dictionary with an
automatically induced one (unsupervised) | Tests sensitivity to dictionary
quality |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Retriever size: Remove contrastive alignment entirely (train on
word-level MLM only, no bilingual signal).

2 Confidence threshold: Vary the threshold (0.5,0.7,0.85,0.95) to measure
precision–recall trade-off on retrieved pairs.
3 Dictionary size: Reduce dictionary from5k →1k →200 entries to measure how
much bilingual signal the retriever needs.
4 Negative sampling strategy: Compare random negatives vs. in-batch negatives
vs. hard negative mining via TF-IDF similarity.
5 Monolingual data quantity: Subset source/target monolingual data from5M →500k
→50k sentences.
6 NMT model scale: Increase NMT to12-layer/1024-dim to test whether gains
persist in larger models.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|---|---|---| | Retriever yields no high-confidence pairs (<50k) | Medium —
depends on how well dictionary covers the monolingual data | Fall back to a
weaker threshold (0.5) and filter by round-trip consistency instead; if still
<50k, report ablation (A2) to characterize the threshold boundary | | Augmented
data is too noisy and degrades BLEU | Low–Medium — random retrieval baseline
(B5) bounds noise, and contrastive retrieval should be better than random |
Measure per-pair confidence and stratify test-set BLEU by retrieval confidence
quartiles; if low-confidence pairs actively hurt, use confidence-weighted
training loss | | Dictionary quality is poor (many incorrect entries) | Low for
Wiktionary; Medium for automatically induced dictionaries | B6 ablation tests
this explicitly; if Wiktionary exists for the language pair, use it; if not,
report the induction baseline separately | | Gains appear only on small NMT
model, vanish at scale | Medium — larger models have stronger language priors
and may not benefit from extra data | Ablation A6 tests this directly; if gains
vanish, reframe contribution as "efficient retrieval for small models" | |
Computational budget (1 GPU-day) is insufficient | Low — the small encoder and
modest NMT are designed to fit this budget | Profile training step time; if
close to the limit, reduce monolingual data to2M sentences and cap NMT epochs
at30 | | Results are language-pair specific | Medium — gu-en may be easy due to
shared script in some domains, or hard due to limited data quality | Replicate
on a second language pair (kk-en) with distinct script and different data
sources; report both in the main paper |

question: Help me generate a research proposal on AI for software engineering.
answer_a:
A Controlled Study of Automated Program Repair via Iterative Research Synthesis
   with and without Cross-Run Memory Evolution## TitleIterative Research for
     Automated Program Repair: An Ablation of Cross-Run Memory Evolution in
                          Scientific Discovery Agents

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemLarge language models have achieved impressive results on isolated code
generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP), yet their application to scientific
research on program repair — where the goal is not merely to write a fix but to
discover, validate, and report a reproducible repair method — remains
underexplored. Current approaches treat each research session as independent,
discarding accumulated knowledge about which repair strategies fail or succeed
across different bug classes. The central question is whether cross-run memory
evolution (preserving and reusing validated ideas, validation criteria, and
experimental strategies across sessions) meaningfully improves the quality and
efficiency of program repair research compared to isolated single-run efforts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisA research agent equipped with cross-run evolution mechanisms
(idea-direction memory, idea-validation memory, and experiment-strategy memory)
will produce higher-quality program repair proposals — measured by repair
success rate, reproducibility of reported results, and novelty of the proposed
method — than an otherwise identical agent that operates as a non-evolving
single-run system. Furthermore, the advantage will grow as the number of
research iterations increases.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodWe compare two variants of the EvoScientist research agent applied to the
task of automated program repair:

Full EvoScientist (FS): The agent receives a program repair task, conducts
literature grounding, generates candidate repair ideas across multiple personas
(innovator/pragmatist/critic), ranks them via an ELO tournament, expands the top
idea into a proposal, designs and executes experiments, and writes a final
report. Between runs, the FS variant updates three persistent memory stores: (1)
idea-direction memory — which repair strategies (e.g., semantic patching,
test-suite amplification, invariant inference) have been promising or
unpromising for different bug types; (2) idea-validation memory — which
validation criteria consistently separate strong from weak ideas; (3)
experiment-strategy memory — which experimental setups, hyperparameter ranges,
and evaluation protocols have proven reliable. All three memories are read at
the start of each new run and updated after each completion.

No-Evolution Ablation (FS⁻ᵃˡˡ): The same agent architecture, task pipeline, and
tool use, but all three memory mechanisms are disabled. Each run begins from a
blank slate: no record of prior research directions, no accumulated validation
knowledge, and no cached experimental strategies. The agent must re-explore the
idea space, re-derive validation heuristics, and re-discover experimental
protocols from scratch on every invocation.

Both variants run10 independent program repair tasks sampled from the Defects4J
benchmark (see below). Each variant receives exactly the same prompts, budget,
and tool access.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / BenchmarkDefects4J (v2.0): A curated corpus of835 real Java bugs
from17 open-source projects. We sample10 bugs stratified by project and severity
(5 single-edit bugs from the "Chart", "Lang", "Math", "Closure", and "Time"
projects;5 multi-edit bugs from the same projects). Each bug includes a failing
test case, the passing test suite, and the known fix. Bugs are held out and
never seen by the model during prior training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | Repair Precision | Fraction of bugs for which the proposed method
produces a correct fix (passes all tests in the suite). | | Proposal Novelty |
Semantic overlap between the proposed repair strategy and the top-3 related
works returned by a literature search (lower overlap = higher novelty), scored
by an independent evaluator. | | Experimental Reproducibility | Binary flag:
whether the final report includes all information needed to replicate the
experiment (random seed, exact model configuration, evaluation command,
environment specification). | | Research Efficiency | Total number of tool calls
and search steps consumed per completed proposal (lower is better). | |
Self-Correction Rate | Fraction of runs where the agent detects a flaw in its
own initial experiment (e.g., data leakage, metric miscalculation, confounding
variable) and adjusts before the final report. |

All metrics are reported as means with95% confidence intervals across10
independent runs per variant.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Full EvoScientist (FS): The unablated system with all three
evolution mechanisms active. This is the positive control.

 2 FS⁻ᵃˡˡ (This Proposal): The no-evolution ablation, serving as the negative
   control.
 3 Static Retrieval-Augmented Prompt: A simpler baseline that prepends a static,
   hand-curated document of "best practices for program repair research" to each
   run, without any run-specific memory evolution. This controls for the base
   value of any additional context versus evolved context.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations (within FS⁻ᵃˡˡ)

Since the primary ablation in this study is the removal of all evolution, we
also define three intermediate ablations for completeness (to isolate which
memory component drives any observed advantage):

 • FS⁻ᵈʳ̈ⁱʳ̈ᵗⁱᵒⁿ: Disable only idea-direction memory. Validation and strategy
   memories remain active.
 • FS⁻ᵛᵃˡⁱᵈᵃᵗⁱᵒⁿ: Disable only idea-validation memory. Direction and strategy
   memories remain active.
 • FS⁻ˢᵗʳᵃᵗᵉᵍʸ: Disable only experiment-strategy memory. Direction and
   validation memories remain active.

If the full -all ablation shows a significant drop relative to FS, these
intermediate ablations will pinpoint which memory type contributes most to the
gap.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Task ceiling effect. Defects4J fixes are well-studied;
even the single-run variant may perform at ceiling, obscuring the advantage of
evolution. Mitigation: Include the5 multi-edit bugs, which are substantially
harder and known to saturate simpler approaches.

 2 Memory contamination across runs in FS. Despite stratification, an early-run
   repair method might incidentally help on a later bug via shared patterns
   (e.g., both involve null-pointer guards), making it difficult to attribute
   improvement solely to memory. Mitigation: Log which memory entries are read
   on each run and measure the semantic similarity between the retrieved
   memories and the bug at hand.
 3 Metric noise from model stochasticity. Temperature sampling produces variance
   in idea generation and ranking. Mitigation: Run3 seeds per bug (30 total runs
   per variant) and report confidence intervals.
 4 Reproducibility metric ceiling. Single-run agents may produce equally
   reproducible reports if the report-writing skill is stable regardless of
   memory. Mitigation: Add a fine-grained reproducibility checklist (11 binary
   items adapted from the ML Reproducibility Checklist).
 5 Overfitting to Defects4J. Results may not transfer to other languages or bug
   repositories. Limitation: Explicitly noted as a scope constraint; the
   conclusion will flag replication on BugsInPy and CodeFlaws as necessary
   follow-up.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations- Single benchmark scope. Defects4J covers only Java bugs from a
specific set of projects. Generalization to other languages (Python, JavaScript,
C) and to industrial codebases is not tested.

 • Fixed budget per run. Both variants receive identical compute budgets. It is
   possible that an evolving system's advantage lies in reallocating budget more
   intelligently over time — a benefit that a same-budget comparison may
   underestimate if the evolution mechanism itself consumes resources.
 • No human-in-the-loop. The evaluation measures the proposal as produced by the
   agent, not the downstream utility of that proposal when executed by a human
   researcher. An agent that produces a slightly lower-scoring but more readable
   proposal might be more useful in practice.
 • Short horizon (10 runs). Evolution mechanisms may require more runs to show
   significant compound effects. A100-run study would be needed to estimate the
   asymptotic benefit.
 • Confounding between memory types. The three memory mechanisms interact:
   better experiment strategies may produce cleaner results that in turn feed
   better validation criteria. A full factorial design (2³ =8 conditions) would
   separate main effects from interactions but is beyond the scope of this
   Table3 ablation.

Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report
results conditioned on specification clarity.
4 Test generation cost — Generating k test cases per problem × n samples ×
repair iterations is significantly more expensive than sampling alone.
Mitigation: report token cost per solved problem; treat this as a proposed
quality-cost tradeoff.
5 Model self-attribution bias — The model may be overly agreeable with its own
generated tests, failing to challenge its code against rigorous oracles. The
cross-model ablation (tests from model A, code from model B) tests this
directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Experimental Protocol1. For each problem, generate self-specification
tests (k=20) from the docstring.

2 Draw100 code samples per problem (pass@k evaluation).
3 For each sample passing original tests: run self-generated tests; flag
failures.
4 Attempt repair (up to3 iterations) on each flagged candidate.
5 Evaluate final correctness against HumanEval+ extended tests (ground truth).
6 Report: pass@k (baseline), added-correctness (method), self-gap, repair
recovery, over-repair rate, token cost per problem.

Table3 Ablation -all: Non-Evolving Single-Run Research Proposal## TitleMetaEval:
 A Calibrated Multi-Dimensional Framework for Accurate Automated LLM Evaluation

ProblemAutomated evaluation of Large Language Models — using metrics like BLEU,
ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore, and LLM-as-Judge (e.g., GPT-4, Claude, or open-source
judges like Prometheus) — suffers from systematic inaccuracies:

 1 Reference-metric saturation: Lexical overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) plateau
   and misorder outputs once generation quality surpasses a moderate threshold.
   They penalize valid paraphrases and reward surface-form similarity over
   semantic correctness.
 2 LLM-as-Judge biases: Position bias (preferring the first candidate),
   verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), self-enhancement bias (preferring
   outputs from the same model family), and intra-model consistency are
   well-documented but not reliably corrected.
 3 Task-specific metric collapse: On code generation, reasoning, and math,
   pass@k and execution-based checks have high resolution but narrow coverage;
   semantic metrics fail to capture functional correctness. On open-ended
   generation, no single metric correlates reliably with human judgment across
   domains.
 4 Absence of uncertainty-aware aggregation: Point estimates of evaluation
   scores are reported without calibration or confidence intervals, making it
   impossible to distinguish genuine gains from evaluation noise.

The research question is: Can a multi-dimensional evaluation framework with
explicit bias correction, per-dimension calibration, and uncertainty-aware
aggregation produce evaluations that correlate with human judgment more
consistently than any single existing metric or LLM judge?

HypothesisA meta-evaluation framework that (a) scores model outputs across four
disjoint dimensions — factual accuracy, instruction following, fluency, and
efficiency — using separate calibrated probes per dimension, (b) applies
per-probe debiasing transforms learned from a small human-annotated calibration
set, and (c) aggregates dimension scores with a Bayesian hierarchical model that
outputs posterior distributions (not point estimates), will achieve a Spearman
correlation with pooled human judgments ≥0.85 on held-out evaluation data,
exceeding the best single-metric baseline (GPT-4-as-Judge) by ≥0.08.

MethodMetaEval is designed as a four-stage pipeline, with no evolutionary
component — each stage is static and defined upfront:

Stage1 — Multi-Dimension Decomposition. Define four evaluation dimensions
formalized as scoring rubrics:

 • Factual Accuracy: Proportion of claims in the output supported by the
   provided context or world knowledge. Scored0–3 per claim, averaged.
 • Instruction Following: Binary or graded checklist of request constraints
   (length, format, tone, content restrictions). Scaled0–1 per constraint.
 • Fluency: Perplexity under a small LM (e.g., TinyLlama) + grammatical error
   rate. Normalized0–1.
 • Efficiency: Output length / required length ratio penalized by verbosity
   threshold. Scaled0–1.

Stage2 — Calibrated Probe Assignment. Each dimension is scored by a different
lightweight evaluator LLM fine-tuned on that dimension only (LoRA fine-tuned
from a7B base, e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct). The four probes share no parameters.
Training data:2,000 human-annotated examples per dimension from the evaluation
benchmark.

Stage3 — Per-Probe Debiasing. For each probe, compute a debiasing transform on a
held-out calibration set (500 examples):

 • Fit a linear correction: corrected_score = α · raw_score + β, where α, β are
   dimension-specific, optimized to minimize mean squared error against human
   scores on the calibration set.
 • Optionally fit a dimension-wise position-bias correction: score each
   candidate in both orders (A→B, B→A) and average.

Stage4 — Bayesian Aggregation. The four corrected dimension scores per output
are combined via a hierarchical Bayesian model:

 • Likelihood: s_d ~ Normal(μ_d, σ_d²) for each dimension d.
 • Prior: flat (no cross-run updates — fixed at initialization).
 • Posterior output: Overall Score = Σ w_d · μ_d with credible intervals, where
   weights w_d are estimated from human preference data.
 • Report: posterior mean +90% credible interval, enabling uncertainty-aware
   comparisons.

Dataset / BenchmarkEvalHarvest — a composite benchmark assembled from four
existing evaluation suites, ensuring diversity across evaluation paradigms:

 1 MT-Bench (multi-turn chat, open-ended):80 multi-turn queries with human
   preference judgments.
 2 AlpacaEval2.0 (single-turn instruction following):805 examples with
   length-controlled win rates.
 3 CodeEval (HumanEval+) (functional correctness):164 problems with both pass@1
   and human pass/fail judgments.
 4 TruthfulQA (factual accuracy):817 questions with human-reviewed truthfulness
   scores.

Total: ~1,860 annotated examples. Split:2,000 (Stage2 training),500 (Stage3
calibration),1,360 (Stage4 evaluation held-out). The held-out set has ≥3 human
annotators per example (majority-vote ground truth).

Evaluation MetricsPrimary metric:

 • Spearman's ρ between MetaEval's posterior mean score and pooled human
   judgments on the held-out set (n =1,360).

Secondary metrics:

 • Kendall's τ (more robust to ties) for the same comparison.
 • Per-dimension Spearman ρ to diagnose which dimensions drive agreement.
 • Coverage of90% credible interval: proportion of human judgments falling
   within the CI (calibration check).
 • Metric dispersion: standard deviation of scores across five random seeds of
   probe training, to measure sensitivity.

Baselines1. BLEU — lexical overlap baseline (unweighted average of BLEU-1
through BLEU-4).

 2 ROUGE-L — longest common subsequence recall.
 3 BERTScore (DeBERTa-large) — reference-based semantic similarity.
 4 GPT-4-as-Judge (direct) — single prompt instructing GPT-4 to score on a1–10
   scale (no rubric decomposition).
 5 GPT-4-as-Judge (rubric) — same with a detailed scoring rubric per dimension,
   averaging dimension scores.
 6 Prometheus2 (7B) — open-source LLM judge fine-tuned for evaluation, used
   as-is.
 7 Single-Probe MetaEval (ablation of the multi-probe design): one evaluator LLM
   scores all four dimensions at once.

All baselines report Spearman ρ against the same held-out human judgments.

Ablations1. -probes: replace four specialized probes with a single general probe
scoring all dimensions (isolates the value of decomposition).

 2 -debias: skip the per-probe debiasing transform (isolates the value of
   calibration).
 3 -bayesian: replace Bayesian aggregation with a simple arithmetic mean of
   dimension scores (isolates the value of uncertainty-aware weighting).
 4 -dimensions: score on a single aggregate rubric (no decomposition) using the
   best-performing single probe (isolates the value of multi-dimension design).
 5 -all (this variant): non-evolving single-run proposal — no cross-run memory,
   no iterative refinement of the framework parameters or rubric definitions.
   The design above is frozen before evaluation begins.

Expected Failure Modes1. Probe specialization collapse: The four fine-tuned
probes may produce highly correlated scores despite being trained on separate
dimensions, reducing the benefit of decomposition. Mitigation: enforce
orthogonality via contrastive loss during fine-tuning (requires a validation
check on probe score covariance).

 2 Calibration set mismatch: If the500-example calibration set does not cover
   the distribution of errors in the held-out set, the per-probe debiasing could
   overfit and reduce held-out performance. Mitigation: stratify calibration
   sampling by domain and output length.
 3 Bayesian prior specification: Without evolution memory to inform prior
   parameters, the flat priors may produce wide credible intervals that reduce
   discriminability (overlap between systems). Mitigation: report posterior
   overlap matrices in addition to point rankings.
 4 Fluency dimension ceiling: Most LLM outputs in the benchmark are already
   highly fluent, making the fluency dimension nearly constant and effectively
   reducing the framework to three dimensions. Mitigation: if fluency variance
   <5% of total variance, drop it and report a3-dimension version as a
   sensitivity analysis.
 5 Position bias in probes: Even after the A→B / B→A averaging correction,
   residual position bias may persist if probe preference is asymmetric across
   dimensions. Mitigation: compute δ = score(A→B) − score(B→A) as a diagnostic
   and flag examples where |δ| >0.2 for manual review.

Limitations1. No evolutionary adaptation: The framework is frozen at deployment.
If evaluation standards shift (e.g., new evaluation dimensions become relevant),
the full pipeline must be retrained. A memory-enabled system would incrementally
adapt its rubric and debiasing transforms across evaluation cycles.

 2 Language and scale dependence: The calibration set and probe training use
   English-only data at ≤7B parameter scale. The effectiveness of the
   per-dimension decomposition on non-English or multilingual evaluation, or
   with larger judges (70B+), is not tested.
 3 Human annotation ceiling: The primary metric (Spearman ρ against human
   judgments) is bounded by inter-annotator agreement. If the pooled human
   judgments themselves have low agreement (≤0.80 Fleiss' κ), then even a
   perfect evaluation framework would appear to cap out. The benchmark's actual
   inter-annotator agreement is reported but not controlled.
 4 Cost: Four fine-tuned probes × inference on each candidate increases
   evaluation cost approximately4× over a single LLM judge. For most research
   use cases this is acceptable, but large-scale leaderboard evaluations would
   require cost optimizations (e.g., cascading: run only until a confident
   decision is reached per dimension).
 5 No generative improvement: This proposal addresses measurement accuracy, not
   generation quality. Improving evaluation accuracy does not directly improve
   model outputs — it only makes ranking and selection more reliable. A full
   research program would pair improved evaluation with training-time reward
   shaping, which is outside scope.

Research Proposal: Addressing Accuracy Issues in Automated LLM Evaluation---

Title
Calibrated Ensemble Evaluation (CEE): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy
through Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Model Deliberation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based automated evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge") are the dominant method
for evaluating open-ended text generation at scale, but suffer from four
well-documented accuracy issues:

1 Systematic biases — position bias (preferring first or second response),
verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-enhancement bias
(preferring outputs from models similar to the judge).
2 No uncertainty quantification — standard practice returns a point estimate
(score or preference) with no confidence, making it impossible to know when
the judge is uncertain vs confident.
3 Low inter-rater reliability — agreement between LLM judges and human raters
varies wildly across domains (Spearman ρ ranges from0.3 on creative writing
to0.7 on factual QA).
4 Rubric brittleness — even with detailed rubrics, LLM judges often fail to
follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

The core unmet need is an evaluation framework that produces trustworthy scores
— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing evaluation into atomic quality criteria, aggregating
judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated
set will significantly improve accuracy — defined as Spearman rank correlation
with held-out human judgments — over the standard single-model, single-pass,
holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method (3-stage pipeline)

Stage1: Atomic Criterion DecompositionInstead of asking a judge for a single
"overall quality" score (which collapses heterogeneous dimensions), decompose
evaluation into6 atomic rubrics:

#  Criterion              Definition
1  Relevance              Does the response address the prompt directly?
2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)
3  Coherence              Is the response logically structured and internally
consistent?
4  Completeness           Does the response cover the scope requested?
5  Conciseness            Is the response free of unnecessary verbosity?
6  Instruction Following  Does the response obey format, length, and style
constraints?

Each criterion is scored on a1–5 Likert scale by each evaluator model, using a
criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and
the response. This prevents any single criterion from dominating.

Stage2: Multi-Model Panel with UncertaintyQuery a panel of K =3 to5 diverse LLM
evaluators (from different model families, e.g., GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet,
Llama370B, Gemini2.0 Flash, Mistral Large). Each model scores each response on
all6 criteria.

For each (model, criterion, response) triple, also extract the log-probability
of the score token(s) as a proxy for the model's confidence in that judgment.
This gives a per-criterion confidence weight.

Stage3: Calibration LayerUsing a held-out calibration set of N =500–1,000
examples with human ratings on the same6 criteria (collected from3 annotators
per example):

1 Score Aggregation: Per criterion, compute a confidence-weighted average
across models: s_c = Σ_i w_i_c * score_i_c / Σ_i w_i_c where w_i_c =
exp(logprob_i_c) is model i's confidence on criterion c.
2 Bias Correction: Fit a small logistic regression or isotonic regression per
criterion to map the aggregated score s_c to a calibrated score ŝ_c that
minimizes expected calibration error against human ratings.
3 Uncertainty Output: For each response, output both the calibrated score
vector ŝ ∈ [1,5]^6 and a per-criterion uncertainty interval derived from the
weighted variance across the panel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Use | Size | Human Annotations |

|---------|-----|------|-------------------| | MT-Bench | Primary evaluation |80
multi-turn questions,3,360 model outputs | Human preference + pairwise ratings
(published) | | Chatbot Arena (subset) | Primary evaluation |10K randomly
sampled comparisons | Human preference votes (public) | | FLASK | Fine-grained
evaluation | ~1,700 model outputs | Human ratings on12 fine-grained dimensions |
| ShareGPT + rubric annotation | Calibration set |500 examples,3 annotators/ex |
Collected fresh (6 atomic criteria + overall) | | AlpacaEval2.0 | OOD test |805
examples | Length-controlled win rates (indirect human signal) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it measures | Target |

|--------|-----------------|--------| | Spearman ρ (with human scores) | Rank
correlation — primary metric | >0.65 (vs ~0.50–0.55 for GPT-4 baseline on
creative/ open-ended tasks) | | Exact + Adjacent Agreement | Score-level match
with humans | >60% exact +85% adjacent | | Position Bias Rate | % of trials
where swapping A/B order flips the preference | <5% (vs ~15–20% for single-model
judges) | | Verbosity Correlation | Pearson r between predicted score and
response length (log tokens) | |r| <0.10 (vs ~0.35 for rubric-free judges) | |
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration of confidence vs accuracy
| <0.08 | | Test-Retest Consistency | Variance across3 independent runs on same
input | σ² <0.02 per criterion | | Cost per Evaluation | API cost per evaluation
@ inference time | Report in USD for transparency |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why chosen |

|----------|-------------|------------| | GPT-4-as-a-judge (holistic) | Single
GPT-4 call scoring "overall quality"1–5 | De facto standard in most LLM
evaluation pipelines | | GPT-4-as-a-judge (with rubric) | Same model, but with
the6 atomic criteria in prompt | Controls for rubric decomposition effect alone
| | PairRM | Trained pairwise reward model (based on Llama) | Representative of
trained, task-specific evaluators | | JudgeLM | Fine-tuned evaluator on100K
human judgments | Strongest published fine-tuned baseline | | Majority Vote (3x)
| Same model (GPT-4) called3 times, majority vote | Controls for the effect of
repeated sampling alone | | Humans (held out) | Human judgment on held-out test
set | Upper-bound oracle (no automated evaluation is expected to match this, but
it anchors the comparison) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations
Each ablation removes or varies one component of CEE while holding
everything else fixed, tested on the MT-Bench test set:

Ablation                 Variation                  What it isolates
Panel size               K =1 vs3 vs5 models        Value of model diversity
Criterion decomposition  Replace6 criteria with     Value of atomic rubric
single holistic "overall"  structure
judgment
Uncertainty weighting    Replace                    Value of log-prob
confidence-weighted        confidence signal
average with uniform
average
Calibration layer        Remove calibration (use    Value of human-anchored
raw aggregated scores)     calibration
Model diversity          Same-family panel (GPT-4o  Value of cross-family
×3) vs cross-family        diversity vs repeated
(GPT-4o + Claude + Llama)  sampling

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|-------------|-----------|------------| | Calibration overfitting — the
calibration layer overfits to the small (500-example) human set and degrades on
OOD distributions like AlpacaEval | Medium | Use regularization (isotonic
regression with smoothing); report OOD performance separately; scale calibration
set to1,000 if budget permits | | Model collinearity — diverse models produce
correlated errors on the same failure cases (e.g., all miss subtle factual
errors in stylized text) | Medium-High | Analyze error correlation matrix across
models; if collinearity is high (>0.8 across all pairs), consider subsampling to
the two most independent models | | Criterion decomposition misses holistic
qualities — atomic rubrics fail to capture emergent dimensions (interestingness,
novelty, tone) that drive human preferences | Medium | Add a7th "overall
gestalt" criterion alongside atomic ones; check whether the holistic dimension
is needed for high human correlation via ablation | | Computational cost — K ×6
API calls per evaluation (e.g.,5 ×6 =30 calls) is15–30× more expensive than a
single-judge baseline, limiting practical adoption | High | Accept cost as a
trade-off for research-phase accuracy; report cost per evaluation; investigate
whether pruning to the top-2 criteria after a pilot study can reduce calls3×
with minimal accuracy loss | | Rubric leakage — models exhibit new
criterion-specific biases (e.g., always giving "conciseness" low scores to long
but good answers) | Medium | Exploratory analysis of per-criterion score
distributions; adjust rubric wording in a small pilot (N=50) before finalizing |
| Human annotation bottleneck — collecting500 ×6 ×3 ≈9,000 reliable
atomic-criterion annotations is expensive and slow | High | Use existing FLASK
dataset (already has fine-grained annotations) to bootstrap; only collect ~200
fresh annotations for the calibration held-out set | | Log-prob confidence is
poorly calibrated — score-token log-probs may not reflect true judgment
confidence, especially under sampling temperature >0 | Medium | Set temperature
to0 for evaluation calls; if log-probs still unreliable, replace with
self-reported confidence ("How confident are you in this score on a1-5 scale?")
as an alternative confidence signal |
